sentences: You are at the Lahori Gate, the way in.
Shah Jahan built it facing Lahore, which is how it got its name.
The wall you are looking at ends in bastions at both corners, each one crowned by a pavilion.
The screen wall in front of the gate is not his.
Aurangzeb added it, and his father wrote to him from prison in Agra to say that he had made the Fort a bride and set a veil before her face.
It is not clear whether that was meant as a compliment.
Every fifteenth of August the Prime Minister speaks to the country from the rampart above you.
This is the Chatta Chowk, the covered bazaar.
It runs two hundred and thirty feet, and there are thirty two arched rooms along the sides of it.
They were shops then and they are shops now.
Halfway along, the roof opens into an octagonal court about thirty feet across, and that is the only thing letting light and air into the whole passage.
Look up at the plaster around that opening and you can still find traces of the painting that once covered it.
Fergusson called this the noblest entrance belonging to any palace still standing.
The Naubat Khana, the drum house.
This was the main way into the court of the Diwan-i-Aam, and it was the point at which you got off your elephant.
Everybody did, except princes of the blood royal.
It was called the Hathia Pol, the elephant gate, for that reason.
Above the gateway there is an open hall of five arched bays, and that is where the musicians sat.
They played at fixed hours, so this building told the time as well as guarding the door.
You are standing in front of the Diwan-i-Aam, the hall of public audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648 and held his first court here soon after.
It is built entirely of red sandstone, and it was once covered in gilding and painted plaster, all of which is gone.
Inside, four columns carry each arch, in seven bays across three aisles.
In the middle of the far wall there is a recess raised above the floor.
That is where the Emperor sat.
The lawn in front of you stands in for a courtyard that ran five hundred and sixty feet.
The shrubberies mark where the arcades used to be, and every morning they were full of men waiting to be seen.
This is the Rang Mahal, the painted palace.
It is named for the colour that once covered the inside of these walls, and almost none of it is left.
Shah Jahan knew it as the Imtiyaz Mahal, the palace of distinction, and it was the largest apartment in the imperial household.
A marble channel runs the length of the floor, and at its centre sits a basin cut from a single block of Makrana marble.
The ceiling was silver first, then copper, then wood.
Each replacement was a smaller claim than the one before.
Behind you, between this hall and the back of the Diwan-i-Aam, there was a walled garden with a tank at its centre.
It lay buried until 1911, when it was uncovered again.
This is the Khas Mahal, where the Emperor actually lived.
Three rooms face the Diwan-i-Khas, three more behind them were the sleeping chamber, and the hall alongside held the wardrobe and the treasury.
The walls carry a dado of inlaid marble.
Look at the screen on the north wall.
It was cut out of a single slab, and the pattern in it is a pair of scales hanging over a crescent moon among stars and clouds.
That is the Mizan-i-Adl, the scales of justice, and it was put where anyone bringing a complaint would see it.
The inscriptions on the arches were written by Sadullah Khan, who ran the government of Shah Jahan until he died in 1656.
This is the Diwan-i-Khas, the hall of private audience.
Shah Jahan finished it in 1648, and a nineteenth century surveyor called it the most highly ornamented building he ever put up.
Look at the lower part of the piers.
Every piece of coloured stone in them was cut to fit a socket chiselled out of the marble.
Higher up, the arches were gilded and painted.
The marble channel running down the centre of the floor was called the Nahr-i-Bihisht, the stream of paradise.
The peacock throne stood on the dais in this room until 1739, when Nadir Shah carried it away to Persia.
He accepted the surrender of the Mughal Emperor here first, and took the throne afterwards.
The Hammam, the royal baths.
Three main rooms divided by corridors, and every surface you would have touched is marble inlaid with coloured stone.
The pavements, the reservoirs, the slabs the steam came through, and the walls up to waist height.
The room facing the river was where you undressed.
It has three fountain basins in it, and one of them ran rose water.
Some of the coloured glass in the window lattice is original.
Heating this building was said to take a hundred and twenty five maunds of firewood, which is something over four tonnes.
The Moti Masjid, the pearl mosque.
Aurangzeb built it about eleven years after the Fort was finished, and it cost a hundred and sixty thousand rupees of the time.
It was private.
The Emperor prayed here, and so did the women of the household, who reached it by their own passage through the north wall.
The doors on the east side are plated with copper.
The domes are wrong.
The originals were covered in gilded copper, they were damaged in 1857, and what you are looking at is the repair.
The Hayat Bakhsh Bagh.
The name means life bestowing.
It was laid out with the rest of the Fort, quartered by water channels in the Persian manner.
Then it was lost.
By 1902 the whole garden was under earth, rubble and roads, and the channels had almost completely gone.
Digging it back out took from 1904 to 1911.
Only half of it came back, because the army had built barracks on the other half.
Almost everything you can see of the causeways and the channels is reconstruction.
Mumtaz Mahal, eighty eight feet by eighty two.
This was one of the apartments of the seraglio, the part of the palace where the women of the household lived.
The lower parts of the walls and piers are marble, and traces of the painted and glass decoration that covered the rest have been uncovered.
The gilded chhatris that stood at the corners of the roof are gone.
What happened to this building afterwards is roughly what happened to the whole Fort.
It was a prison after 1857, then a sergeants mess, and it is a museum now.
